source_text: Γυνή τις συνεβίου ἀνδρὶ ἀκολασταίνοντι, ἀκολασταίνουσα καὶ αὐτὴ πρότερον. Ἐπεὶ δὲ τὰ τοῦ Χριστοῦ διδάγματα ἔγνω, αὐτὴ ἐσωφρονίσθη καὶ τὸν ἄνδρα ὁμοίως σωφρονεῖν πείθειν ἐπειρᾶτο, τὰ διδάγματα ἀναφέρουσα, τήν τε μέλλουσαν τοῖς οὐ σωφρόνως καὶ μετὰ λόγου ὀρθοῦ βιοῦσιν ἔσεσθαι ἐν αἰωνίῳ πυρὶ κόλασιν ἀπαγγέλλουσα. Ὁ δὲ ταῖς αὐταῖς ἀσελγείαις ἐπιμένων ἀλλοτρίαν διὰ τῶν πράξεων ἐποιεῖτο τὴν γαμετήν. Ἀσεβὲς γὰρ ἡγουμένη τὸ λοιπὸν ἡ γυνὴ συγκατακλίνεσθαι ἀνδρί, παρὰ τὸν τῆς φύσεως νόμον καὶ παρὰ τὸ δίκαιον πόρους ἡδονῆς ἐκ παντὸς πειρωμένῳ ποιεῖσθαι, τῆς συζυγίας χωρισθῆναι ἐβουλήθη. Καὶ ἐπεὶ ἐξεδυσωπεῖτο ὑπο τῶν αὐτῆς, ἔτι προσμένειν συμβουλευόντων, ὡς εῖς ἐλπίδα μεταβολῆς ἥξοντός ποτε τοῦ ἀνδρός, βιαζομένη ἑαυτὴν ἐπέμενεν. Ἐπειδὴ δὲ ὁ ταύτης ἀνὴρ εἰς τὴν Ἀλεξάνδρειαν πορευθεὶς χαλεπώτερα πράττειν ἀπηγγέλθη, ὅπως μὴ κοινωνὸς τῶν ἀδικημάτων καὶ ἀσεβημάτων γένηται μένουσα ἐν τῇ συζυγίᾳ καὶ ὁμοδίαιτος καὶ ὁμόκοιτος γινομένη, τὸ λεγόμενον παρ᾿ ὑμῖν ῥεπούδιον δοῦσα ἐχωρίσθη. Ὁ δὲ καλὸς κἀγαθὸς ταύτης ἀνήρ, δέον αὐτὸν χαίρειν, ὅτι, ἃ πάλαι μετὰ τῶν ὑπηρετῶν καὶ τῶν μισθοφόρων εὐχερῶς ἔπραττε, μέθαις χαίρουσα καὶ κακίᾳ πάσῃ, τούτων μὲν τῶν πράξεων πέπαυτο καὶ αὐτὸν τὰ αὐτὰ παύσασθαι πράττοντα ἐβούλετο, μὴ βουλομένου ἀπαλλαγείσης κατηγορίαν πεποίηται, λέγων αὐτὴν Χριστιανὴν εἶναι. Καὶ ἡ μὲν βιβλίδιόν σοι τῷ αὐτοκράτορι ἀναδέδωκε, πρότερον συγχωρηθῆναι αὐτῇ διοικήσασθαι τὰ ἑαυτῆς ἀξιοῦσα, ἔπειτα ἀπολογήσασθαι περὶ τοῦ κατηγορήματος μετὰ τὴν τῶν πραγμάτων αὐτῆς διοίκησιν, καὶ συνεχώρησας τοῦτο. Ὁ δὲ ταύτης ποτὲ ἀνήρ, πρὸς ἐκείνην μὲν μὴ δυνάμενος τανῦν ἔτι λέγειν, πρὸς Πτολεμαῖόν τινα, ὃν Οὔρβικος ἐκαλέσατο, διδάσκαλον ἐκείνης τῶν Χριστιανῶν μαθημάτων γενόμενον ἐτράπετο διὰ τοῦδε τοῦ τρόπου. Ἑκατόνταρχον εἰς δεσμὰ ἐμβαλόντα τὸν Πτολεμαῖον, φίλον αὐτῷ ὑπάρχοντα, ἔπεισε λαβέσθαι τοῦ Πτολεμαίου καὶ ἀνερωτῆσαι, εἰ, αὐτὸ τοῦτο μόνον, Χριστιανός ἐστι. Καὶ τὸν Πτολεμαῖον, φιλαλήθη ἀλλ᾿ οὐκ ἀπατηλὸν οὐδὲ ψευδολόγον τὴν γνώμην ὄντα, ὁμολογήσαντα ἑαυτὸν εἶναι Χριστιανόν, ἐν δεσμοῖς γενέσθαι ὁ ἑκατόνταρχος πεποίηκε, καὶ ἐπὶ πολὺν χρόνον ἐν τῷ δεσμωτηρίῳ ἐκολάσατο. Τελευταῖον δέ, ὅτε ἐπὶ Οὔρβικον ἤχθη ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ὁμοίως αὐτὸ τοῦτο μόνον ἐξητάσθη, εἰ εἴη Χριστιανός. Καὶ πάλιν, τὰ καλὰ ἑαυτῷ συνεπιστάμενος διὰ τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ διδαχήν, τὸ διδασκάλιον τῆς θείας ἀρετῆς ὡμολόγησεν. Ὁ γὰρ ἀρνούμενος ὁτιοῦν ἢ κατεγνωκὼς τοῦ πράγματος ἔξαρνος γίνεται, ἢ ἑαυτὸν ἀνάξιον ἐπιστάμενος καὶ ἀλλότριον τοῦ πράγματος τὴν ὁμολογίαν φεύγει· ὦν οὐδὲν πρόσεστι τῷ ἀληθινῷ Χριστιανῷ. Καὶ τοῦ Οὐρβίκου κελεύσαντος αὐτὸν ἀπαχθῆναι, Λούκιός τις, καὶ αὐτὸς ὢν Χριστιανός, ὁρῶν τὴν ἀλόγως οὕτω γενομένην κρίσιν, πρὸς τὸν Οὔρβικον ἔφη· Τίς ἡ αἰτία, τοῦ μήτε μοιχὸν μήτε πόρνον μήτε ἀνδροφόνον μήτε λωποδύτην μήτε ἅρπαγα μήτε ἁπλῶς ἀδίκημά τι πράξαντα ἐλεγχόμενον, ὀνόματος δὲ Χριστιανοῦ προσωνυμίαν ὁμολογοῦντα τὸν ἄνθρωπον τοῦτον ἐκολάσω; Οὐ πρέποντα Εὐσεβεῖ αὐτοκράτορι οὐδὲ φιλοσόφῳ Καίσαρος παιδὶ οὐδὲ τῇ ἱερᾷ συγκλήτῳ κρίνεις, ὦ Οὔρβικε. Καὶ ὃς οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἀποκρινάμενος καὶ πρὸς τὸν Λούκιον ἔφη· Δοκεῖς μοι καὶ σὺ εἶναι τοιοῦτος. Καὶ τοῦ Λουκίου φήσαντος· Μάλιστα, πάλιν καὶ αὐτὸν ἀπαχθῆναι ἐκέλευσεν. Ὁ δὲ καὶ χάριν εἰδέναι ὡμολόγει, πονηρῶν δεσποτῶν τῶν τοιούτων ἀπηλλάχθαι γινώσκων καὶ πρὸς τὸν πατέρα καὶ βασιλέα τῶν οὐρανῶν πορεύεσθαι. Καὶ ἄλλος δὲ τρίτος ἐπελθὼν κολασθῆναι προσετιμήθη.
thought_title: A Christian Woman's Divorce and Persecution
pass_a_gloss: A certain woman lived with a husband who was licentious, and she herself was licentious before. But when she learned the teachings of Christ, she became self-controlled and tried to persuade her husband to be self-controlled in the same way, referring to the teachings and announcing the punishment that will be in eternal fire for those who live unself-controlled and with wrong reasoning. But he, persisting in the same licentiousness, made the wife foreign to him through his actions. For the woman, considering it impious to lie together with a husband who, contrary to the law of nature and what is right, tries to make pleasure from every source, wanted to separate from the marriage. And when she was being persuaded by her own people to still wait, advising her to wait in hope of the husband's change, she forced herself to endure. But when it was reported that her husband, having gone to Alexandria, was doing worse things, so that she might not become a sharer in his injustices and impieties by remaining in the marriage and becoming a partner in the same bed and table, she gave the divorce paper, as it is called among you, and separated. But the good and noble husband of hers, who ought to have been glad that she had stopped the actions which she previously did easily with the servants and hired workers, taking pleasure in drunkenness and all evil, and that she wanted him to stop doing the same things, brought a charge against her, saying she was a Christian. And she handed over a petition to you, the emperor, asking to be allowed to manage her own affairs first, and then to make a defense concerning the charge after managing her affairs, and you allowed this. But the husband of hers, not being able to speak to her anymore, turned to a certain Ptolemy, who had been called by Urbicus, and who had become a teacher of Christian teachings to her. He, having thrown Ptolemy into prison, a friend of his, persuaded him to take Ptolemy and ask him if he was a Christian. And Ptolemy, being a lover of truth but not deceitful or a liar, having confessed that he was a Christian, was put in prison by the centurion, and was punished for a long time in the prison. Finally, when the man was brought before Urbicus, he was examined on this one thing only, if he was a Christian. And again, knowing the good things in himself through the teaching from Christ, he confessed the teaching of divine virtue. For the one who denies or condemns anything becomes a renouncer or considers himself unworthy and foreign to the matter, and flees from the confession, which is of no use to the true Christian. And when Urbicus ordered him to be led away, a certain Lucius, who was also a Christian, seeing the unreasonable judgment, said to Urbicus: What is the reason that this man, who has been convicted of neither adultery nor prostitution nor murder nor theft nor robbery nor any injustice, but has confessed to the name of Christian, has been punished? You are not judging, oh Urbicus, in a way fitting for a pious emperor or a philosophical son of Caesar or a sacred council. And he, answering nothing else, said to Lucius: You seem to me to be the same kind. And Lucius said: Certainly. And again, he ordered Lucius to be led away. But he confessed, knowing that he was grateful to have escaped evil masters of this kind and to be going to the Father and King of the heavens. And another, a third, came forward and was deemed worthy of punishment.

pass_b_english: A woman once lived with a licentious husband, and she herself had formerly been licentious as well. When she learned the teachings of Christ, she became self-controlled and tried to persuade her husband to practice the same self-control, citing those teachings and warning him of the eternal fire awaiting those who live without self-control and right reason. He, however, persisted in the same licentiousness and, through his actions, made his wife a stranger to him. Since she considered it impious to continue sharing a bed with a husband who, contrary to the law of nature and what is right, sought to make pleasure from every possible source, she wanted to separate from the marriage. When her own people urged her to wait longer, advising that her husband might yet change, she forced herself to endure. But when it was reported that her husband, after going to Alexandria, was committing even worse acts, she gave him the divorce paper — what you call a *repudium* — and separated, so that she would not become a partner in his injustices and impieties by remaining in the marriage and sharing bed and board.

Her excellent husband — who should have been glad that she had stopped the deeds she once easily committed with servants and hired workers, indulging in drunkenness and every evil, and that she wanted him to stop doing the same — brought a charge against her, saying she was a Christian. She presented a petition to you, Emperor, asking first to be allowed to manage her own affairs and then to make her defense concerning the charge after that management was complete; you granted this request. Her husband, no longer able to confront her directly, turned to a certain Ptolemy, whom Urbicus had summoned, and who had become her teacher in the Christian doctrines. He had a centurion throw Ptolemy, his own friend, into prison, then persuaded the centurion to take Ptolemy and ask him only this: whether he was a Christian. Ptolemy, a lover of truth but neither deceitful nor a liar, confessed that he was a Christian; the centurion put him in chains and punished him for a long time in prison. Finally, when Ptolemy was brought before Urbicus, he was examined on that one point alone: whether he was a Christian. Again, knowing the good things in himself through the teaching from Christ, he confessed the teaching of divine virtue. For anyone who denies or condemns anything becomes a renouncer, or considers himself unworthy and alien to the matter and flees from the confession — neither of which belongs to the true Christian.

When Urbicus ordered him to be led away, a certain Lucius, also a Christian, seeing the unreasonable judgment, said to Urbicus: "What is the reason that this man, who has been convicted of neither adultery nor prostitution nor murder nor theft nor robbery nor any injustice, but has only confessed to the name of Christian, has been punished? You are not judging, Urbicus, in a manner fitting for a pious emperor, or a philosophical son of Caesar, or a sacred council." Urbicus answered nothing else but said to Lucius: "You seem to me to be the same kind." Lucius replied: "Certainly." And again Urbicus ordered him to be led away. Lucius confessed with gratitude, knowing that he had escaped evil masters of that sort and was going to the Father and King of the heavens. And another, a third, came forward and was deemed worthy of punishment.
